title: Learning Options for Compositional Motor Control with Adapter Banks
claim: Low-rank perturbations of a shared recurrent network can place eigenvalues at chosen targets, selectively producing distinct frequency-specific dynamics.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right: schematic, eigenvalue plot, stacked time series, color-coded motifs
description: Three-panel figure. Panel A is a schematic: a large gray circle labeled Cortical RNN holds a few recurrently connected nodes. Below it, four colored elongated loops (cyan, magenta, magenta, blue) end in small colored circles, labeled Low-Rank Thalamic Adapters. Black curved arrows link the adapters to the cortex in both directions. Panel B is a complex-plane scatter titled Induced Eigenvalues. A gray disc of cortex eigenvalues sits near the origin, and a red dashed vertical line marks Re=1. Four colored star pairs sit on that line at conjugate frequencies ω1 to ω4, with a legend. Panel C, Activity per Adapter, shows five stacked time series over 0–25. The gray J0 trace is noisy and aperiodic. The four colored traces J0+u_k v_k^T oscillate at progressively higher frequencies, with colors matching panel B.
caption: Adapter Banks as Thalamocortical Loops (A) Schematic of the framework of [ref]: thalamic inputs $u_k$ drive a cortical RNN with recurrence $J_0$. A rank-one perturbation $u_k v_k^\top$ can induce oscillatory dynamics at a target frequency. (B) Eigenvalue placement. Gray: eigenvalues of the bare cortex $J_0$. Stars: target locations on the oscillation line (Re$(\lambda) = 1$) for four motifs at different frequencies $\omega_k$. Each low-rank perturbation shifts a conjugate pair of eigenvalues to the corresponding target. (C) Cortical activity projected onto a one-dimensional readout. Each motif $J_0+u_kv_k^{T}$ sustains a different oscillation at its target frequency $\omega_k$, demonstrating that rank-one perturbations selectively recruit the cortical network to produce frequency-specific dynamics.
abstract: Learning flexible motor primitives is a hallmark of skilled motor control. Recent neuroscience theory proposes that motor primitives may be implemented as low-rank perturbations of a shared recurrent network, but leaves open how such a system is learned. We translate this principle into a novel architecture for learning motor skills end-to-end: a shared recurrent core modulated by a bank of residual adapters, each selected by a discrete latent code. Trained on closed-loop biomechanical control, the adapters develop emergent low-rank perturbations of the recurrent dynamics despite no architectural rank constraint, placing task representations in disparate subspaces of the shared core network. A simple high-level policy over the learned options, optimized while the whole network is frozen, sequences the low-rank adapters to produce novel out-of-distribution movements. We demonstrate the ability to generalize to novel motor sequences within the closed-loop control setting, improving on the generalization error of a task-input-conditioned multitask baseline by approximately sevenfold.
